_note: agent-b fixture · REAL output of POST /audit for MyFlashLoanReceiver (aave-v3-flashloan-receiver) with the AAVE-FL-001 mitigation deleted — this is demo step 4's state. Restoring it returns every finding to mitigated. Regenerate with: npm run fixtures:refresh.

findings.title: Flash-loan callback is not gated to the Pool AND the initiator
findings.summary: Anyone can call Pool.flashLoan naming your contract as the receiver, so Aave invokes your callback on the attacker's behalf.
findings.detail: Developers treat executeOperation as private because 'only Aave calls it'. Checking msg.sender == Pool is necessary but not sufficient: the Pool will happily call any receiver address a third party names. Without also requiring initiator == address(this), an attacker funds a flash loan, points it at your contract, and your callback runs with their amount, their premium and their params. Every subsequent gate in the contract is then operating on attacker-chosen state.
findings.remediation: Require all three gates in executeOperation: msg.sender == address(POOL), initiator == address(this), and a contract-owned reentrancy/inflight flag set by your own entrypoint before calling flashLoanSimple.

findings.title: Idle funds held on a flash-loan receiver
findings.summary: If your receiver holds a balance, an attacker's flash loan is repaid out of your money.
findings.detail: Aave PULLS amount + premium from the receiver after executeOperation returns. A receiver with an idle balance therefore repays any flash loan that names it, so a third party can borrow, do nothing, and let your treasury pay the premium. Aave's own documentation warns about exactly this. Note that a correct AAVE-FL-001 initiator gate already blocks the third-party path, since the callback rejects loans this contract did not initiate; an explicit balance assertion is defence in depth.
findings.remediation: Sweep to zero at the end of every operation and assert the contract holds no idle balance of the flash-loaned asset outside an in-flight operation.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled calldata executed from inside the callback
findings.summary: Decoding a target address and a calldata blob out of `params` and calling it turns a callback bug into a full drain.
findings.detail: The common aggregator pattern decodes (address target, bytes data) from params, approves target for the maximum, then does target.call(data). Combined with AAVE-FL-001 the attacker supplies both halves and the contract signs its own approval away. Even with the callback correctly gated, an arbitrary-call sink lets any privileged caller move every token the contract has ever been approved for.

incidents.name: Mimo SuperVault aggregatorSwap(dexTxData) — arbitrary external call

findings.remediation: Never take a call target or calldata from params. Restrict routers to an owner-managed allowlist, restrict the selector, and approve the exact amount for the exact call then reset it to zero.

findings.title: eMode price-source divergence
findings.summary: In eMode Aave may value assets with a category price source, so your quote and Aave's quote disagree.
findings.detail: An eMode category can define its own priceSource. When priceSource == address(0) Aave falls back to the per-asset oracle, otherwise the category feed overrides it for every asset in the category. An integration that always calls getAssetPrice(asset) will therefore size borrows against a different price than the one used at liquidation, and the gap is exactly the attacker's margin.
findings.remediation: Resolve the user's eMode category, use the category priceSource when it is non-zero, and fall back to the per-asset oracle only when it is address(0).

findings.title: Oracle scale / decimals mismatch
findings.summary: Aave prices are quoted in the oracle base unit, not in the token's own decimals, so unscaled maths mis-sizes every borrow.
findings.detail: AaveOracle returns prices denominated in BASE_CURRENCY_UNIT (1e8 for the USD base currency), while USDC has 6 decimals and WETH has 18. Multiplying a raw balance by a raw price without normalising both sides is off by many orders of magnitude, and the error direction decides whether you under-borrow harmlessly or open an instantly liquidatable position.
findings.remediation: Normalise explicitly: value = amount * price * 10**baseDecimals / (10**assetDecimals * BASE_CURRENCY_UNIT), and read decimals() from the token rather than hardcoding it.

findings.title: Aave's risk engine re-implemented more permissively than Aave
findings.summary: Locally re-deriving borrowing capacity ignores eMode, isolation mode, siloed borrowing, debt ceilings and the reserve config bitmap.
findings.detail: Integrations frequently compute 'how much can I borrow' from collateral value times LTV. Aave's own accounting is strictly more restrictive: isolation-mode debt ceilings, siloed reserves, eMode category caps and freeze/pause bits all bind first. A wrapper that is more permissive than the protocol it wraps will originate positions that are already unhealthy the moment they land.
findings.remediation: Never re-derive capacity. Read Pool.getUserAccountData after the action and revert unless healthFactor stays above your own floor (strictly greater than 1e18). Only applies to contracts that actually borrow.

findings.title: LTV-0 aToken poison dust can freeze withdrawals
findings.summary: One wei of a zero-LTV aToken transferred to your contract can block every subsequent withdrawal.
findings.detail: Aave applies a stricter validation path once an account holds any collateral whose LTV has been set to zero: withdrawals and collateral disabling revert while debt exists. Because aTokens are ERC20-transferable, an attacker griefs the integration for the cost of 1 wei plus gas. Two things defuse it: never carrying debt (Aave only runs the LTV check when the account is borrowing), and an escape hatch that can move a foreign aToken back out.

incidents.name: StErMi — Aave v3 LTV-0 bug bounty writeup

findings.remediation: Either keep the position debt-free (Aave only enforces the zero-LTV rule while borrowing) or expose an access-controlled escape hatch that can move a foreign aToken out. Reading the reserve configuration bitmap before withdrawing lets you surface the condition explicitly.

findings.title: Missing minAmountOut on the swap leg
findings.summary: A swap with a zero minimum-out is a standing invitation to a sandwich bot.
findings.detail: Leverage loops and deleverage paths almost always contain a swap. Passing amountOutMinimum: 0 (or computing it on-chain from the same pool being traded against) means the entire trade can be sandwiched for its full value. This is the single most-tagged DeFi class in the registry with 120 instances.

incidents.name: vuln/defi/slippage — 120 tagged PoCs in the registry

findings.remediation: Take minAmountOut as a caller-supplied parameter derived off-chain, or derive it from the Aave oracle price with an explicit bounded slippage tolerance — never from the pool you are trading against.

findings.title: Unchecked external call / transfer return values
findings.summary: Non-standard ERC20s return false instead of reverting, and a discarded low-level call result hides the failure entirely.
findings.detail: USDT and friends do not return a bool from transfer/approve, so a bare call either reverts on decode or silently succeeds depending on the compiler. A low-level .call(...) whose success flag is discarded turns a failed transfer into a successful-looking state update. Both patterns show up 90 times in the registry under vuln/dependency.

incidents.name: Aave portal loan repayment not enforced (registry PoC)

findings.remediation: Use OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 (safeTransfer / forceApprove) for every token movement and check the success flag of every low-level call.

findings.title: Supply/borrow caps, pause and freeze cause unhandled reverts
findings.summary: A reserve that is capped, frozen or paused makes supply/borrow revert, and a leverage loop mid-flight bricks.
findings.detail: Aave governance can pin a supply cap to the current utilisation, freeze a reserve, or pause the whole pool. Integrations that assume supply always succeeds will revert in the middle of a multi-step position, leaving collateral posted and debt open. The failure must be detected before the state-changing sequence begins, not discovered halfway through it.

incidents.name: Sherlock Index #267 — supply cap causes revert

findings.remediation: Pre-flight the reserve configuration for caps, freeze and pause bits, and revert with a named error before any state change.

findings.title: No ERC20 escape hatch for non-principal tokens
findings.summary: Airdrops, Merkl rewards and mistaken transfers land on the contract and are stuck forever.
findings.detail: Every long-lived DeFi integration eventually receives a token it was not designed to hold. Without a sweep function those assets are permanently frozen. The sweep must be authorised and must refuse the principal asset and the aToken, otherwise the escape hatch becomes the exploit.

incidents.name: Morpho integration checklist — escape hatch requirement

findings.remediation: Add an access-controlled sweep(token, to) that reverts for the underlying asset and its aToken.
